kf1.tip: Think of something you forgot this week, then decide whether encoding, storage or retrieval was the weak link and give one reason for your choice.
kf1.note: A strong answer ties the evidence to one process. If the memory came back later, perhaps after a reminder or a tip-of-the-tongue moment, it was stored, so retrieval was the weak link, most likely because a cue was missing. If you only repeated it without thinking about what it meant, surface encoding is the better choice, because shallow encoding fades quickly. The trap is naming a process without saying what tells you it was that one.

kf2.tip: Choose a sport or hobby you do and write one example from it of episodic memory, one of semantic memory and one of procedural memory.
kf2.note: A good answer has three clearly different examples. Episodic must be a personal event tied to a time and place, such as one particular match you played. Semantic must be a general fact or rule you know without recalling when you learned it. Procedural must be a skill you perform without thinking through the steps. Check you have not mixed them up: remembering the day you learned a skill is episodic, but doing it automatically is procedural.

cs1.tip: Predict whether you would recall your first day at secondary school better standing in the school or sitting at home, and explain why using retrieval cues.
cs1.note: You would most likely recall it better standing in the school. The memory is already stored, but retrieval needs the right cue to unlock it. Being in the school gives context cues, such as the place itself and perhaps its smells. These link to an episodic memory tied to that time and place. At home those cues are missing, so the memory is more likely to stay out of reach.
